name: Load balancers
summary: Spreads incoming traffic across healthy servers.
howItWorks: A load balancer gives a service one stable address and forwards each request or connection to one of several backends. It runs health checks and stops sending traffic to failed instances, terminates TLS, and lets you add or remove servers without clients noticing. It picks a backend with an algorithm such as round robin, least connections or hashing. Layer 4 balancers forward TCP and UDP connections; layer 7 balancers understand HTTP and can route by host name or path.
analogy: The host at a busy restaurant, seating each new party with a waiter who’s free and skipping the section that’s closed.
useWhen: Running more than one copy of any service
Zero-downtime deploys: drain old instances, add new ones
avoidWhen: A single instance with no redundancy; it adds cost and little else
Cross-region failover on its own; that needs DNS or a global balancer
example: Three API servers sit behind an Application Load Balancer. When server 2 fails its `/health` check twice in a row, the balancer stops routing to it, and users only ever see the other two answer.

source: location / { proxy_pass http://api; }   # round robin by default

diagram.caption: Requests are handed out in turn across three servers. When server 2 fails its health check, it’s skipped until it recovers.

story: When early websites outgrew one machine, the first trick was round-robin DNS: publish several server addresses under one name and rotate their order. It spread load, but DNS had no idea whether a server was alive. If one failed, the DNS kept handing out its address, and caches meant clients kept trying it.

The fix was a box in front of the servers. Cisco’s LocalDirector was conceived in late 1995, when Netscape’s webmaster described customers whose round-robin DNS left some servers swamped and others idle. It reached its first customers in 1996. Such appliances gave a site one virtual address and mapped each connection to one of the servers behind it. Software caught up: the Linux Virtual Server project started in 1998, Willy Tarreau began writing HAProxy in 2000, and nginx’s first public release followed in 2004.

Large operators then moved load balancing back onto ordinary machines. Google has run Maglev, a load balancer built from commodity Linux servers, since 2008. In 2009 AWS made load balancing a managed service with Elastic Load Balancing, and its layer-7 Application Load Balancer arrived in 2016.

choices.choice: One virtual address in front of many servers
choices.why: Clients only ever see the balancer’s address, so servers can be added, removed or patched behind it without anyone updating DNS or client configuration.

choices.choice: Health checks decide where traffic goes
choices.why: Round-robin DNS kept sending users to dead servers. A balancer that probes each backend stops using a failed one after a few missed checks.

choices.choice: Layer 4 for speed, layer 7 for smarts
choices.why: Forwarding TCP connections without reading them is fast and works for any protocol. Reading HTTP costs more CPU but allows routing by host or path, TLS termination and retries.

choices.choice: Software on commodity servers instead of appliances
choices.why: Google built Maglev this way because it needs no special rack deployment and capacity grows by adding servers. Cloud load balancers work on the same principle.

timeline.text: Cisco LocalDirector ships, an early dedicated load-balancing appliance
